questions.stem: The famous 'Dancing Girl' figurine excavated from Mohenjo-daro is fashioned from which material using the lost-wax (cire-perdue) casting technique?

options.option_text: Steatite (soapstone), a soft grey metamorphic rock
Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, cast by lost-wax
Terracotta, sun-dried and kiln-fired river clay
Carnelian, a semi-precious red-orange gemstone

questions.explanation: The Dancing Girl (~2500 BCE) is a bronze statuette made via the lost-wax (cire-perdue) casting method — the earliest known lost-wax bronze from the subcontinent. Steatite is the material for IVC seals, not this figurine. Terracotta was used for the Mother Goddess figurines, not this piece.

questions.stem: Indus Valley Civilization seals were primarily carved from which raw material, which craftsmen then fired and glazed to harden the surface?

options.option_text: Bronze, shaped and polished for ritual trade purposes
Terracotta, fired at high kiln temperatures for strength
Steatite (soapstone), carved then glazed after firing
Sandstone, quarried near major Indus river settlements

questions.explanation: Over 2,000 IVC seals have been recovered; the vast majority are carved from steatite (soapstone), a soft stone easy to engrave, which was then fired and coated with an alkali glaze to produce a hard white surface. Bronze was used for figurines; terracotta for Mother Goddess statuettes and toys.

questions.stem: Which animal motif appears most frequently across all excavated Indus Valley seals and is regarded as the signature iconographic symbol of the civilisation?

options.option_text: Humped zebu bull, linked to later Vedic cattle worship
Unicorn (one-horned bull) shown before a ritual filter stand
Elephant depicted in ceremonial procession-style scenes
Swamp deer, sacred to the Pashupati figure on seals

questions.explanation: The unicorn — a bull with a single curved horn depicted before an object scholars call a 'filter stand' or 'incense burner' — is the most common motif, appearing on roughly 60% of IVC seals. The humped bull is frequent but secondary. The unicorn's function and the object before it remain subjects of scholarly debate, making this an examiner favourite.

questions.stem: Indus Valley pottery is archaeologically identified by a characteristic colour scheme. Which combination correctly describes the dominant decorative style of this pottery?

options.option_text: White geometric motifs painted on a black-glazed clay body
Red and yellow alternating horizontal bands on buff ware
Black painted designs applied over a red-slipped clay body
Blue and white floral patterns impressed on pale buff ware

questions.explanation: IVC pottery is characteristically 'red ware with black painting' — the clay body receives a red slip and black geometric or natural (pipal leaf, fish, peacock) designs are painted over it. Blue-and-white pottery is associated with later Mughal-era traditions; white-on-black is not an IVC convention.

questions.stem: The Indus site of Lothal (Gujarat) is archaeologically significant as a major production centre for which category of craft objects that were widely traded across contemporary civilisations?

options.option_text: Steatite seals engraved with pictographic Indus script
Fired terracotta figurines of the Mother Goddess type
Carnelian, shell, and faience beads for long-distance trade
Copper fish-hooks and net-weights for maritime commerce

questions.explanation: Lothal housed a dedicated bead-making workshop; evidence includes unfinished carnelian beads, polishing stones, and a furnace. Lothal beads (especially the long barrel-cylindrical carnelian type) have been found in Mesopotamia. Lothal is also known for its dockyard, but bead manufacture is its signature craft industry in art-history questions.

questions.stem: The 'Priest-King' bust excavated from Mohenjo-daro wears a shawl with a specific repeated decorative motif. Which motif, confirmed by pigment traces in the carved recesses, covers this garment?

options.option_text: Fish-scale pattern carved in alternating horizontal register rows
Trefoil (three-leaf) design with red pigment inlay in each cell
Lotus medallion arranged in concentric circular petal bands
Swastika symbols arranged diagonally across the draped shawl

questions.explanation: The Priest-King bust (c. 2000 BCE, steatite, ~17.5 cm, now in Karachi Museum) has a trefoil/shamrock design incised across his robe, with red pigment surviving in the recesses — indicating the pattern was originally filled with red paste or inlay. Fish-scale and lotus patterns are IVC pottery motifs, not documented on this bust. The trefoil also appears on similar Central Asian objects of the same period, suggesting interregional artistic links.

questions.stem: IVC seals possess a distinctive structural feature on their reverse side that scholars use to infer their administrative rather than purely decorative function. What is this feature, and what does it indicate?

options.option_text: A flat polished back engraved with ownership or clan markings
A perforated boss (knob) used to thread a cord for carrying or stamping
A recessed groove cut along the edges for tying a wax cord
A raised border ridge that retained wet clay during seal impressions

questions.explanation: On the reverse of almost every IVC seal is a prominent boss (knob or handle) with a hole drilled through it. This perforation allowed the seal to be threaded on a cord and worn, or pressed easily into wet clay to seal goods — confirming their role as mercantile or administrative tokens. The boss distinguishes IVC seals from contemporary Mesopotamian cylinder seals, which are rolled rather than stamped.
